content: Taribavirin, also known by its International Nonproprietary Name (INN) as well as the name viramidine and the codename ICN 3142, is an antiviral drug currently undergoing Phase III clinical trials in humans. However, it has not yet been approved for pharmaceutical use. This compound is a prodrug of ribavirin, meaning it is metabolized into ribavirin in the body, and it exhibits activity against a variety of DNA and RNA viruses. Taribavirin demonstrates improved liver-targeting properties compared to ribavirin. It has a shorter half-life in the body due to reduced penetration and storage in red blood cells. This pharmacokinetic profile makes it a promising candidate for the treatment of viral hepatitis syndromes where ribavirin is effective. These conditions include hepatitis C and potentially hepatitis B and yellow fever. In animal models, taribavirin has shown antiviral activity against influenza that is comparable to ribavirin, but with slightly reduced toxicity. This suggests that taribavirin may eventually replace ribavirin as a preferred anti-influenza agent. The drug is being developed by Valeant Pharmaceuticals International, the parent company of Ribapharm, which first reported the synthesis and testing of taribavirin in 1973. Valeant is currently investigating taribavirin as a treatment for chronic hepatitis C. From a chemical perspective, taribavirin contains a carboxamidine group, which is somewhat basic. As a result, the drug is also formulated and administered as its hydrochloride salt, which has a distinct chemical formula and corresponding ChemID/PubChem identifiers. At physiological pH, partial protonation of the carboxamidine group imparts a positive charge to the molecule. This charge slows the drug's ability to cross cell membranes, such as those of red blood cells, until it is metabolized into ribavirin. In the liver, the conversion of the carboxamidine group to a carboxamide group occurs during first-pass metabolism. This transformation contributes to the higher concentrations of ribavirin observed in liver cells and bile when taribavirin is administered. This liver-specific targeting enhances its therapeutic potential for liver-related viral infections.
